addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- amazon-bedrock: Builds generative AI applications on Amazon Bedrock. Covers model invocation (Converse API, InvokeModel), RAG with Knowledge Bases, Bedrock Agents, Guardrails, and AgentCore. Use when invoking models, setting up Knowledge Bases, creating agents, applying guardrails, deploying to AgentCore, troubleshooting Bedrock errors (ThrottlingException, AccessDeniedException), or choosing models (Claude, Llama, [infra], Titan). ALSO USE for prompt caching setup and debugging, quota health checks and throttling diagnosis, cost attribution and tracking, migrating between Claude model generations (4.5 to 4.6 to 4.7), chunking strategies, API selection (Converse vs InvokeModel), guardrail capabilities, and model selection. Also covers AgentCore Payments setup (x402, microtransactions, Payment Manager, Connector, Instrument, Coinbase CDP, Stripe Privy, 402 Payment Required, pay for content, paid endpoint, agent payments). NOT for custom model training, Rekognition, or Comprehend.
- aws-billing-and-cost-management: Analyze AWS costs, find savings, manage budgets, evaluate Savings Plans and Reserved Instances, right-size EC2/Lambda/RDS/EBS with Compute Optimizer, look up service pricing, query CUR with Athena, detect cost anomalies, scope costs to billing views, and monitor Free Tier usage. Triggers on: AWS bill, cost analysis, reduce spend, savings plan, reserved instance, right-size, budget alert, cost optimization, pricing, free tier, cost anomaly, CUR, cost audit, billing view, billing view ARN.
- aws-blocks: Guides building full-stack applications with AWS Blocks — an Infrastructure-from-Code framework. Applies when creating APIs, selecting Building Blocks (KVStore, DistributedTable, Database, AuthBasic, AuthCognito, Realtime, AsyncJob, FileBucket, etc.), running local development, or deploying AWS Blocks applications. Also covers AWS Blocks topics with validated, version-specific patterns that prevent common mistakes. Triggers when user mentions AWS Blocks; project has aws-blocks/ directory; code imports @aws-blocks packages.
- aws-cdk: Authors, deploys, and troubleshoots AWS infrastructure using CDK with TypeScript or Python. Covers best practices, stack architecture, and construct patterns. Always use when writing CDK constructs, bootstrapping environments, running cdk deploy/synth/diff, fixing CDK or CloudFormation errors, planning stack structure, importing existing resources, resolving drift, or refactoring stacks without resource replacement.
- aws-cloudformation: Author, validate, and troubleshoot AWS CloudFormation templates. Covers template authoring with secure defaults, pre-deployment validation (cfn-lint, cfn-guard, change sets), and root-cause diagnosis of failed stacks using CloudFormation events and CloudTrail correlation.
- aws-containers: Deploys and operates containerized workloads on ECS, Fargate, and ECR. Covers task definitions, Fargate services, ECR repository setup and lifecycle policies, ECS Exec debugging, service scaling, deployment strategies, load balancer integration, and logging configuration. Use when deploying, debugging, or optimizing containers on AWS. ALSO USE for container deployment options (ECS vs ECS Express Mode), networking modes, health check troubleshooting, OOM errors, secrets injection, blue/green deployments, ECR image management, and App Runner sunset guidance and migration. NOT for Kubernetes, EKS, or CI/CD pipelines.
- aws-messaging-and-streaming: Guides use of AWS messaging and streaming services. Covers Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS, Amazon EventBridge, Amazon MQ, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon Data Firehose, Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, and Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK). Use when implementing messaging and streaming patterns.
- aws-observability: Builds, configures, debugs, and optimizes AWS observability with CloudWatch (Log Insights, Metrics, Alarms, Dashboards, EMF), X-Ray, CloudTrail, and ADOT (AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry), AND enables/onboards services to Application Signals using ADOT auto-instrumentation SDKs. Covers Log Insights queries, alarms (metric, composite, anomaly), dashboards, custom metrics/EMF, X-Ray tracing and sampling, ADOT collector config, CloudTrail auditing, and end-to-end Application Signals enablement via ADOT SDKs (CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on, CloudWatch Agent IAM, OTLP endpoints, ServiceEvents, Dynamic Instrumentation), breakpoint and snapshot in Dynamic Instrumentation, live data capture in running service, debug without redeploying. Applies to CloudWatch, alarms, dashboards, EMF, X-Ray, traces, CloudTrail,  ADOT, monitoring, synthetics/canaries, OR enabling/onboarding/instrumenting a service for Application Signals. Not for app logging or security threat detection.
- aws-sdk-js-v3-usage: AWS SDK for JavaScript v3 development patterns. Use when writing JavaScript or TypeScript code that uses AWS services via @aws-sdk/* packages (aws-sdk-js-v3), or when asked about schemas, runtime validation, serialization, or code generation in the context of the JS/TS AWS SDK.
- aws-sdk-python-usage: AWS SDK for Python (boto3/botocore) development patterns. You MUST use this skill when writing Python code that uses AWS services via boto3 or botocore. This includes creating service clients or resources, configuring sessions and credentials, handling errors with ClientError, using paginators and waiters, S3 file transfers and presigned URLs, DynamoDB table operations, and any boto3/botocore client configuration. Use this skill whenever Python code imports boto3 or botocore, or when the user asks about AWS operations in Python.
- aws-sdk-swift-usage: AWS SDK for Swift development patterns. Use when writing Swift code that uses AWS services via aws-sdk-swift package.
- aws-serverless: Builds, deploys, manages, debugs, configures, and optimizes serverless applications on AWS using Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions, EventBridge, and SAM/CDK. Covers cold starts, CORS debugging, event source mappings, troubleshooting, concurrency, SnapStart, Powertools, function URLs, EventBridge Scheduler, Lambda layers, and production readiness. Triggers on mentions of Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions, SAM templates, CDK serverless stacks, DynamoDB stream triggers, SQS event sources, cold starts, timeouts, 502/504 errors, throttling, concurrency, CORS, Powertools, or any event-driven architecture on AWS, even without the word "serverless." Does not apply to EC2, ECS/Fargate containers, or Amplify hosting.
- cso: Chief Security Officer mode. (gstack)
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- investigate: Systematic debugging with root cause investigation. (gstack)
- office-hours: YC Office Hours — two modes. (gstack)
- review: Pre-landing PR review. (gstack)
- signing-in-to-aws: Gets AWS credentials for CLI/SDK access via `aws login`. Activates when a developer needs to authenticate to AWS for local development, when an AWS operation fails due to missing or expired credentials, or when someone asks about setting up AWS access. Triggers: "set up AWS", "configure AWS", "aws login", "get credentials", "authenticate", "session expired", "token expired", "no credentials", "AccessDeniedException" with no configured credentials.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

content.text: I'll start by reading redu.md.

content.content:
1	---
2	redu_schema: 2
3	repo: https://github.com/seanmorley15/AdventureLog
4	plan:
5	  tool: deploy_compose
6	  image: ghcr.io/seanmorley15/adventurelog:v0.13.0
7	  port: 8015
8	  vm: m1.medium
9	  flavor_id: "3"
10	  database: managed postgres WITH THE POSTGIS EXTENSION (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2", db_extensions ["postgis"])
11	  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0452
12	bootstrap:
13	  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
14	  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
15	  source: adventurelog
16	quirks:
17	  - "USE THE ROOT docker-compose.yml, NOT ONE OF THE OTHER FIVE. The repo ships six compose files and only one of them is the deployment this recipe describes. The root docker-compose.yml is the Standard Deployment: ONE image with the SvelteKit frontend, the Django backend and nginx inside it, on one port. docker/docker-compose.advanced.yml splits it into three containers and needs two public URLs, .dev.yml is for development, .traefik.yaml assumes you terminate TLS yourself, .database.yml is a database on its own, and the file under .github/workflows is a smoke test. Start from the root file and delete its bundled db service, as below."
18	  - "⛔⛔ THIS APP NEEDS POSTGIS, AND redu CAN PROVISION IT, SO DO NOT PUT POSTGRES ON THE APP VM. backend/server/main/settings.py:146 sets the Django ENGINE to django.contrib.gis.db.backends.postgis; a plain Postgres is not a substitute and there is no configuration that makes it one. Pass db_extensions: [\"postgis\"] to deploy_compose alongside database:'managed' and redu installs the postgis-3 package and runs CREATE EXTENSION on the database it provisions, before your container ever starts. ⚠️ VERIFY IT RATHER THAN ASSUMING: redu's extension generator ends every line with || true on purpose, so a failed package install degrades quietly instead of failing the provision. The one command that settles it is in the body of this file, and the failure is at least loud downstream: with the extension missing, migrations fail and the container never becomes healthy."
19	  - "⛔⛔ THE READINESS PROBE AND DJANGO READ THE DATABASE VARIABLES IN OPPOSITE ORDER, AND THAT IS WHAT WILL HANG YOUR DEPLOY. This is the highest-value line in this file. Django takes PGDATABASE before POSTGRES_DB and PGUSER before POSTGRES_USER (settings.py:136-151), so redu's injected values win there and nothing needs remapping. But the entrypoint's own wait-for-postgres takes POSTGRES_USER before PGUSER and POSTGRES_DB before PGDATABASE (docker/shared/entrypoint-common.sh:20-22), and docker/aio/env-setup.sh:19-21 always fills those in with \"adventure\" and \"database\" when they are unset. redu's managed Postgres defaults to database `app` and user `appuser`, so the probe authenticates as a user that does not exist, forever, printing 'PostgreSQL is unavailable - sleeping' once a second while Django itself would have connected fine. THE FIX IS ONE LINE PER VARIABLE: in the compose, set POSTGRES_DB to the injected PGDATABASE, POSTGRES_USER to PGUSER and POSTGRES_PASSWORD to PGPASSWORD. (The alternative is to pass db_name 'database' and db_user 'adventure' to deploy_compose so redu provisions matching names; either works, and doing NEITHER is the failure.)"
20	  - "POSTGRES_PASSWORD IS REQUIRED AND IT OVERWRITES PGPASSWORD. docker/aio/env-setup.sh:24-28 exits 1 with 'POSTGRES_PASSWORD is required for Standard Deployment' when it is empty, and then unconditionally sets PGPASSWORD from it. So passing only redu's injected PGPASSWORD gives you a container that refuses to start, and passing a DIFFERENT value in POSTGRES_PASSWORD silently overrides the correct one. Set POSTGRES_PASSWORD to the injected PGPASSWORD and the problem disappears in both directions."
21	  - "⛔ SET SECRET_KEY EXPLICITLY, OR EVERY RESTART LOGS EVERY USER OUT AND NOTHING WARNS YOU. docker/aio/env-setup.sh:30-32: if SECRET_KEY is unset the entrypoint generates a fresh random one with secrets.token_urlsafe(50) at every container start. The Standard .env.example does not even list the variable, and says everything else is 'derived automatically at startup', which is true and is exactly the trap: derived means NEW each time. Django signs sessions and password-reset tokens with it. Generate one long random value, pass it as SECRET_KEY, and pass the SAME one on every redeploy."
22	  - "⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: AN ADMIN IS CREATED AT DEPLOY TIME FROM ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES, AND THE SHIPPED DEFAULT IS THE WORD ADMIN AS BOTH USERNAME AND PASSWORD. docker/shared/entrypoint-common.sh:39-66 creates a Django superuser from DJANGO_ADMIN_USERNAME, DJANGO_ADMIN_PASSWORD and DJANGO_ADMIN_EMAIL when that username does not already exist, and marks its allauth email address verified so it can log in immediately. docker/aio/env-setup.sh:34-36 defaults all three, and upstream's Standard Deployment page prints the default login in plain text. This is the SAFE shape, deploy-time creation rather than a race with the first visitor, but ONLY if you actually set the values: leave them alone and you have published an instance whose administrator credential is in the documentation. GENERATE AN ALPHANUMERIC PASSWORD, at least 24 characters. Alphanumeric is not fussiness: the password is interpolated into a Python heredoc in that same shell function, so a quote or a backslash is a syntax error, not a login failure."
23	  - "⛔ REGISTRATION IS OPEN BY DEFAULT. settings.py:279 reads DISABLE_REGISTRATION and defaults it to false, so between the deploy going healthy and you noticing, anyone with the URL can create an account. Set DISABLE_REGISTRATION=True. users/adapters.py:22-38 is what enforces it, and it deliberately still allows signup through an invitation link, which is the right way to add the people you actually want. ⚠️ DO NOT VERIFY THIS ON THE FLAG ENDPOINT ALONE. /auth/is-registration-disabled/ returns the value of the setting (users/views.py:64), which is a check that cannot fail: it will report exactly what you configured whether or not the behaviour changed. Verify on the RENDERED /signup page instead, which swaps the form for your message, and the script in the body does that with both halves."
24	  - "WHAT AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST CAN REACH: the landing page, the login and signup pages, /health, the static assets and the public-user listing. AdventureLog has a real permission model behind that, and with registration closed there is no way for a stranger to obtain an account. Adventures, collections and photos are per-user and private unless their owner marks them public. Media is served through an nginx internal location (docker/shared/nginx-aio.conf), so a protected image is not fetchable by guessing its URL."
25	  - "SITE_URL IS THE ONLY URL VARIABLE YOU NEED, AND IT HAS TO BE THE https ONE. docker/aio/env-setup.sh:9-13 derives ORIGIN, FRONTEND_URL, PUBLIC_URL and CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS from it, so setting it correctly configures four things and setting it wrong breaks four things: CSRF rejections on login, OAuth callbacks pointing at localhost, and media URLs that do not resolve. settings.py:191-192 also switch SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE and CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE on ONLY when the value starts with https, so an http value on an https hostname ships cookies without the Secure flag. Generate the dname yourself UP FRONT, in full adventurelog-<8 lowercase alnum>.redu.cloud form, and set SITE_URL to https://<that name> with no trailing slash. A bare label gets a random suffix appended by redu and will not match."
26	  - "⛔ THE FIRST BOOT DOWNLOADS THE WORLD, AND IT IS WHY THE VM IS SIZED THE WAY IT IS. docker/shared/entrypoint-common.sh:69-84 runs download-countries on every start unless SKIP_WORLD_DATA=1. It fetches dr5hn's countries, states and cities dataset (version pinned at settings.py:470) from raw.githubusercontent.com, streams it through a temporary SQLite file into Postgres, and pulls one flag image per country from flagcdn.com into media storage. UPSTREAM'S OWN WORDS: 'first boot may take several minutes; ensure ~2GB RAM is available', and the script treats exit code 137 as an out-of-memory kill and stops the container. So: the VM needs outbound internet to GitHub and flagcdn on first boot, the first boot is minutes not seconds, and redu's health probe must be allowed to wait it out. If it does get OOM-killed, the two remedies are a larger flavor or SKIP_WORLD_DATA=1, the second of which costs you the world-travel feature until you run the command by hand later."
27	  - "PERSIST /code/media OR YOU LOSE EVERY PHOTO AND EVERY FLAG. settings.py:224 defaults MEDIA_STORAGE to local, so trip photos, avatars and the country flags downloaded on first boot all live on the app VM's filesystem, not in Postgres. Without a volume they vanish on the next redeploy while the database still lists them, and the first boot re-downloads every flag. S3 or an S3-compatible bucket is supported as an alternative (MEDIA_STORAGE=s3 plus the AWS_* variables) and is the right answer for anyone storing a lot of photos, but it is a decision to put to the user with its own cost, not a default."
28	  - "PORT 8015 ON THE HOST, 80 IN THE CONTAINER. The image runs its own nginx (docker/shared/nginx-aio.conf) which serves /static/, guards media through an internal location, sends /media, /admin and /accounts to Django on 8000 and everything else to the SvelteKit server on 3000. Publish host 8015 onto container 80 and pass port 8015 to deploy_compose. Do not try to expose Django or the frontend directly: neither serves the whole application on its own. nginx also carries client_max_body_size 100M, which is the real cap on a photo upload."
29	  - "THE HEALTH ENDPOINT IS A REAL ONE, WHICH IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE MOST ARE NOT. GET /health is answered by the frontend (frontend/src/routes/health/+server.ts) and it returns 200 with {\"ok\":true,\"backend\":\"reachable\"} ONLY after it has confirmed Django is reachable, and 503 otherwise. So it is a genuine gate for both halves of the container, and a script can assert on the body rather than on the status code alone."
30	  - "THE MAP NEEDS NO API KEY, AND GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY IS NOT ABOUT TILES. This is the question nobody documents for a travel app, so here is the answer. frontend/src/lib/index.ts:971-975: the DEFAULT basemap is a CARTO GL style served from basemaps.cartocdn.com, voyager in light mode and dark-matter in dark, keyless, and fetched by the VISITOR'S BROWSER rather than by your VM. The style switcher (:860-968) adds OpenStreetMap raster, OpenTopoMap, OpenFreeMap Liberty, more CARTO variants and USGS topo, all keyless too, with terrain elevation tiles from an AWS open-data bucket. ⚠️ ONE option in that list, the MapTiler 3D terrain one, carries a placeholder key whose value literally reads as an instruction to get your own: choose that basemap without supplying a real MapTiler key and you get a blank map, and it is the only way to get one here. GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY (settings.py:473) affects GEOCODING and place search, not tiles; without it those fall back to the OpenStreetMap provider (adventures/geocoding.py), which is a fine default for a personal instance."
31	  - "EMAIL GOES NOWHERE BY DEFAULT, SO THERE IS NO PASSWORD RESET. settings.py:348-349: EMAIL_BACKEND defaults to Django's CONSOLE backend, which prints the message into the container log and delivers it to nobody. settings.py:318 mercifully defaults ACCOUNT_EMAIL_VERIFICATION to none, so this does not block anything on a fresh instance, and the admin account is created with its email pre-verified. But tell the user plainly: until EMAIL_BACKEND=email and the EMAIL_HOST_* variables point at a real relay, 'forgot password' cannot work and the recovery path is the Django admin at /admin."
32	  - "TURN ON THE RATE LIMITS. settings.py:326 defaults ENABLE_RATE_LIMITS to FALSE while upstream's own .env.example comments it 'Recommended for production'. This entry goes on a public hostname, so set ENABLE_RATE_LIMITS=True. It is the difference between a login endpoint anyone can grind and one that pushes back."
33	  - "PIN THE IMAGE. ghcr.io/seanmorley15/adventurelog publishes exactly four tags, and on 2026-08-17 v0.13.0 resolved to the same digest as the rolling one (sha256:«REDACTED:longhex:7e529879») while `beta` was a different image entirely. Pin the version so a redeploy cannot cross a release that changes a default, and so nobody lands on the beta by a typo. Upstream's compose uses the rolling tag; do not copy that part."
34	  - "DELETE THE BUNDLED db SERVICE, ITS depends_on AND ITS VOLUME. The root compose runs postgis/postgis:16-3.5 on the app VM. With database:'managed' redu gives you a Postgres on its own private VM that survives redeploys, and leaving their db service in place means running two databases on one VM with the app talking to whichever one it was pointed at. Remove the service, the `depends_on` block that waits on it, and the postgres_data volume. Keep the adventurelog_media volume."
35	  - "NO migrate_command NEEDED. docker/aio/entrypoint.sh runs wait_for_postgres, then run_migrations, then create_superuser_if_needed, then download-countries, before supervisord starts anything. Passing a migrate_command would run the migrations a second time against a database that is already migrated."
36	  - "SIZING IS AN ESTIMATE, BUT UPSTREAM DOES PUBLISH THE MEMORY NUMBERS AND THEY ARE THE REASON FOR THE FLAVOR. The Standard Deployment page says 'allocate at least 2 GB RAM on first boot; about 1 GB is usually enough afterward', and the entrypoint repeats the 2 GB figure for the world-data import and stops the container on an OOM kill. Those are UPSTREAM'S numbers, not a redu measurement. So m1.small (2 GB) is exactly the documented first-boot floor with nothing left for Ubuntu and the container runtime, which is why this recipe uses m1.medium (2 vCPU / 4 GB, 40 GB disk). The disk matters too: the image is about 1 GB by upstream's own note, the world dataset and every country flag land on the VM, and so does every trip photo. Measure the real idle figure on your run and write it back."
37	  - "THIS FITS THE NO-CARD TRIAL. m1.medium is exactly the trial ceiling for the app VM and the managed database at m1.small is exactly the one allowed managed DB. Nothing here needs a card. Do pass db_flavor_id explicitly: omitting it defaults the database VM to the app flavor, which both costs more and pushes it over the trial ceiling."
38	  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> generate the dname yourself and build the https SITE_URL from it -> generate SECRET_KEY and an alphanumeric admin password -> write docker-compose.yml and .env into one local directory -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the user the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.045/hr, roughly GBP 33 a month including the database, and it fits the no-card trial) and WAIT for their yes -> prepare_upload -> deploy_compose with the source_token, flavor_id '3' (m1.medium), database:'managed', db_engine:'postgres', db_flavor_id:'2', db_extensions:['postgis'], port 8015. Then verify PostGIS and the closed registration before handing over the URL, and hand the admin credential over in the session."
39	  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built from source: the all-in-one image is pulled. Write docker-compose.yml and .env locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo. Pointing deploy_compose at the GitHub URL would make redu build a roughly 1 GB image on the VM that already exists in the registry."
40	  - "LICENCE: GPL-3.0, verified from the LICENSE file, which is the plain GNU General Public License v3 and NOT the Affero variant. That distinction is the whole point for a self-hoster: GPLv3 has no network clause, so running a modified version as a service for other people does not by itself oblige you to publish your changes, whereas the AGPL would. Distributing a modified build still does. Running the official image unchanged obliges you to nothing extra."
41	  - "⛔ NEVER WRITE CREDENTIALS INTO THIS FILE. SECRET_KEY, the database password and the admin password belong to the user and belong in the session. The deploy log records that the default admin credential was replaced and that registration was closed, never the values."
42	  - "AFTERWARDS: pass THIS file to get_deployment as redu_md and write the merged redu_md_markdown back. ⚠️ Do not assume that captured what your run learned: when this file is richer than redu's template the merge returns redu_md_merge_mode 'in_place', which refreshes last_deploy and appends one deploy-log line and NOTHING ELSE. Any new quirk you found has to be added by hand."
43	  - "DELETING IT LEAVES THE DATABASE BEHIND, ON PURPOSE. delete_deployment removes the app VM but keeps the managed Postgres, so trips, locations and accounts survive, and that database keeps billing at GBP 0.0174/hr. ⚠️ The media volume goes with the app VM, so every uploaded photo is destroyed while the rows referencing them survive. Say that plainly before deleting, and use delete_database when the user really means all of it."
44	---
45	
46	# Self-host AdventureLog on redu
47	
48	A travel journal and trip planner that is actually yours: log where you have been on a world map,
49	plan what is next, attach photos and notes. One container on one VM, a managed PostGIS database
50	beside it, and a public HTTPS URL.
51	
52	## What this deploys
53	
54	- **AdventureLog 0.13.0** from its official all-in-one image, pinned: the SvelteKit frontend, the
55	  Django backend and nginx in one container on one m1.medium VM, published on port 8015.
56	- **Managed Postgres with the PostGIS extension**, on its own private VM. AdventureLog cannot run
57	  on a plain Postgres, and redu installs the extension at provision time rather than leaving you
58	  to do it by hand.
59	- A volume on `/code/media`, which holds your photos and the country flags.
60	- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.
61	
62	About GBP 0.045/hour, roughly GBP 33 a month including the database, and it fits inside the no-card
63	free trial.
64	
65	## Deploy
66	
67	Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
68	directory containing this file:
69	
70	    Read redu.md and deploy AdventureLog on redu.
71	
72	The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.
73	
74	## Who is the administrator
75	
76	**An account created at deploy time from three environment variables**, which is the safe shape:
77	there is no race with the first visitor to find the URL. The catch is the other half. Upstream
78	defaults all three to the word `admin` and prints that default login in its own installation
79	guide, so a deploy that leaves them alone publishes an instance whose administrator credential is
80	in the documentation.
81	
82	So this recipe sets `DJANGO_ADMIN_USERNAME`, `DJANGO_ADMIN_PASSWORD` and
83	`DJANGO_ADMIN_EMAIL` to values you generate, and closes registration
84	(`DISABLE_REGISTRATION=True`) so nobody else can sign up afterwards. Invitation links still work,
85	which is how you add the people you actually want.
86	
87	Generate the password **alphanumeric**. It is interpolated into a Python heredoc inside the
88	entrypoint, so a quote or a backslash is a syntax error rather than a login failure.
89	
90	## The three that actually break it
91	
92	**PostGIS.** AdventureLog's Django database engine is the PostGIS one. Point it at a plain Postgres
93	and migrations fail. redu can provision the extension: pass `db_extensions: ["postgis"]`.
94	
95	**The database variable ordering.** Django prefers `PGUSER` and `PGDATABASE`, which is exactly
96	what redu injects. The container's own wait-for-postgres loop prefers `POSTGRES_USER` and
97	`POSTGRES_DB`, which its entrypoint fills in with defaults of its own. Leave that alone and the
98	container waits for a user that does not exist, forever, while Django would have connected fine.
99	The compose below sets both halves to the same values.
100	
101	**`SECRET_KEY`.** Leave it unset and the entrypoint invents a new random one at every start. The
102	app comes up perfectly and logs everybody out.
103	
104	## About the map
105	
106	No API key is needed and none of the tiles come from your VM. The default basemap is a CARTO style
107	fetched by the **visitor's browser**, and the style switcher offers OpenStreetMap, OpenTopoMap,
108	OpenFreeMap and USGS, all keyless.
109	
110	`GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY` is optional and is about **geocoding and place search**, not tiles. Without
111	it, searching for a place falls back to the OpenStreetMap provider, which is fine for a personal
112	instance.
113	
114	The one way to get a blank map here is to pick the **MapTiler 3D terrain** basemap: its URL ships
115	with a placeholder key that literally tells you to get your own. Either supply a real MapTiler key
116	or use one of the other styles.
117	
118	## The compose
119	
120	Two files, in one directory, uploaded together.
121	
122	```yaml
123	services:
124	  app:
125	    image: ghcr.io/seanmorley15/adventurelog:v0.13.0
126	    restart: unless-stopped
127	    environment:
128	      SITE_URL: "${AL_SITE_URL}"
129	      SECRET_KEY: "[REDACTED:value]}"
130	      # Django reads PGDATABASE/PGUSER/PGPASSWORD/PGHOST/PGPORT, which redu injects, first.
131	      # The entrypoint's wait-for-postgres loop reads these THREE first. Same values, both halves.
132	      POSTGRES_DB: "${PGDATABASE}"
133	      POSTGRES_USER: "${PGUSER}"
134	      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
135	      DJANGO_ADMIN_USERNAME: "${AL_ADMIN_USER}"
136	      DJANGO_ADMIN_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
137	      DJANGO_ADMIN_EMAIL: "${AL_ADMIN_EMAIL}"
138	      DISABLE_REGISTRATION: "True"
139	      DISABLE_REGISTRATION_MESSAGE: "Registration is closed on this instance."
140	      ENABLE_RATE_LIMITS: "True"
141	      DEBUG: "False"
142	      GUNICORN_WORKERS: "2"
143	    volumes:
144	      - adventurelog_media:/code/media/
145	    ports:
146	      - "8015:80"
147	    healthcheck:
148	      test: ["CMD", "python3", "-c", "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:80/health')"]
149	      interval: 30s
150	      timeout: 5s
151	      retries: 5
152	      # Generous on purpose: the first boot imports the world dataset before anything answers.
153	      start_period: 600s
154	
155	volumes:
156	  adventurelog_media:
157	```
158	
159	And `.env` beside it, in the same uploaded directory, because `deploy_compose` only ever
160	APPENDS to the project's `.env` and never edits your compose:
161	
162	```env
163	AL_SITE_URL=https://adventurelog-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
164	AL_SECRET_KEY=[REDACTED:value] long random value you generate, reused on every redeploy>
165	AL_ADMIN_USER=<not "admin">
166	AL_ADMIN_EMAIL=<a real address you control>
167	AL_ADMIN_PASSWORD=[REDACTED:value] alphanumeric characters, alphanumeric only>
168	```
169	
170	`PGDATABASE`, `PGUSER`, `PGPASSWORD`, `PGHOST` and `PGPORT` are appended by redu when the
171	managed database is provisioned. You do not write them.
172	
173	## Proving it from outside
174	
175	Run this once the deploy reports ready. Give it the message you configured, so the check has a
176	positive control it cannot fake.
177	
178	```bash
179	#!/usr/bin/env bash
180	# Prove this AdventureLog is fully up and is not taking signups from strangers.
181	#   ./verify-adventurelog.sh adventurelog-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud "Registration is closed on this instance."
182	# Exit 0 = good, 1 = a real problem, 2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting).
183	set -eu
184	HOST="${1:?usage: verify-adventurelog.sh <host> <disabled-message>}"
185	MSG="${2:?pass the DISABLE_REGISTRATION_MESSAGE you configured}"
186	TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT
187	rc=0
188	
189	# 1. GATE. /health is a REAL health check here: the frontend answers 200 only after it has
190	#    confirmed Django is reachable, and 503 otherwise. The first boot imports a world dataset,
191	#    so several minutes of 502 from redu's edge or 503 from the app is "wait", not "broken".
192	code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/health" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/health")
193	if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
194	  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /health answered HTTP $code, not 200." >&2
195	  [ "$code" = "502" ] && echo "  502 from the edge while the container starts. Re-run in a few minutes." >&2
196	  [ "$code" = "503" ] && echo "  503 means the frontend is up but Django is not yet. Still starting, or the" >&2
197	  [ "$code" = "503" ] && echo "  database wiring is wrong: check the container log for 'PostgreSQL is unavailable'." >&2
198	  exit 2
199	fi
200	if ! grep -q '"backend":"reachable"' "$TMP/health"; then
201	  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 200 from /health but the body does not say the backend is reachable." >&2
202	  head -c 200 "$TMP/health" >&2; echo >&2
203	  exit 2
204	fi
205	echo "OK: frontend and Django are both up."
206	
207	# 2. THE ASSERTION, ON THE RENDERED PAGE RATHER THAN ON THE FLAG.
208	#    ⚠️ /auth/is-registration-disabled/ reports the SETTING, so it can only ever tell you what you
209	#    configured. The signup page swaps the form for your message, which is the behaviour itself.
210	code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/signup" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/signup")
211	if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
212	  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /signup answered $code, so nothing below was evaluated." >&2
213	  exit 2
214	fi
215	has_msg=0; has_form=0
216	grep -qF "$MSG" "$TMP/signup" && has_msg=1
217	grep -q 'password1' "$TMP/signup" && has_form=1
218	
219	if [ "$has_form" = "1" ]; then
220	  echo "FAIL: the signup FORM is being served. Anyone with this URL can create an account." >&2
221	  echo "  Redeploy with DISABLE_REGISTRATION=True." >&2
222	  rc=1
223	elif [ "$has_msg" = "1" ]; then
224	  echo "OK: registration is closed, and the page is serving your configured message."
225	else
226	  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: neither the form nor your message is in the page." >&2
227	  echo "  Either the page changed or you passed a different message than you deployed." >&2
228	  echo "  Do not leave this instance up until you have opened /signup and looked." >&2
229	  exit 2
230	fi
231	
232	exit "$rc"
233	```
234	
235	## Proving PostGIS took
236	
237	redu installs the extension with every step ending in `|| true`, deliberately, so a failure
238	degrades quietly rather than failing the whole provision. That means the one thing worth checking
239	is the one thing that cannot be checked by its absence. Run this from the app VM, where the
240	container already has `psql` and the credentials in its environment.
241	
242	```bash
243	# Both halves. The version string is the positive control: an empty result from a command that
244	# never ran looks exactly like an empty result from a database with no PostGIS.
245	sudo docker compose exec -T app sh -c 'psql -h "$PGHOST" -p "${PGPORT:-5432}" -U "$PGUSER" -d "$PGDATABASE" -tAc "SELECT postgis_version();"'
246	# Expect something like "3.5 USE_GEOS=1 USE_PROJ=1 USE_STATS=1". An error mentioning
247	# "function postgis_version() does not exist" means the extension is NOT installed, and the app
248	# will have failed at migrate rather than started.
249	
250	# And the SECRET_KEY, which is the failure that leaves no trace. Print the LENGTH, not the value.
251	sudo docker compose exec -T app sh -c 'printf "SECRET_KEY length: %s\n" "${#SECRET_KEY}"'
252	# A number in the 40s means yours reached the container. Note the entrypoint GENERATES one when
253	# yours is missing, so a plausible length is not by itself proof: compare it across a restart, or
254	# simply confirm the value you set is in the project .env on the VM.
255	```
256	
257	## Licence
258	
259	**GPL-3.0**, and the distinction from AGPL matters here. GPLv3 has no network clause: running a
260	modified AdventureLog as a service for other people does not by itself oblige you to publish your
261	changes. Distributing a modified build still does. Running the official image unchanged obliges you
262	to nothing extra.
263	
264	## Deploy log
265	
266	- Not yet deployed. The first real run replaces this line with its measured time, flavor and
267	  hourly rate, and corrects anything above that turned out to be wrong. The three most useful
268	  things it can add are how long the world-data import actually takes, the idle memory afterwards
269	  against upstream's published 1 GB, and how much of the 40 GB disk the dataset and flags consume,
270	  because this file cites upstream's figures for the first two and guesses at none of them.
271

---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/seanmorley15/AdventureLog
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: ghcr.io/seanmorley15/adventurelog:v0.13.0
  port: 8015
  vm: m1.medium
  flavor_id: "3"
  database: managed postgres WITH THE POSTGIS EXTENSION (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2", db_extensions ["postgis"])
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0452
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: adventurelog
quirks:
  - "USE THE ROOT docker-compose.yml, NOT ONE OF THE OTHER FIVE. The repo ships six compose files and only one of them is the deployment this recipe describes. The root docker-compose.yml is the Standard Deployment: ONE image with the SvelteKit frontend, the Django backend and nginx inside it, on one port. docker/docker-compose.advanced.yml splits it into three containers and needs two public URLs, .dev.yml is for development, .traefik.yaml assumes you terminate TLS yourself, .database.yml is a database on its own, and the file under .github/workflows is a smoke test. Start from the root file and delete its bundled db service, as below."
  - "⛔⛔ THIS APP NEEDS POSTGIS, AND redu CAN PROVISION IT, SO DO NOT PUT POSTGRES ON THE APP VM. backend/server/main/settings.py:146 sets the Django ENGINE to django.contrib.gis.db.backends.postgis; a plain Postgres is not a substitute and there is no configuration that makes it one. Pass db_extensions: [\"postgis\"] to deploy_compose alongside database:'managed' and redu installs the postgis-3 package and runs CREATE EXTENSION on the database it provisions, before your container ever starts. ⚠️ VERIFY IT RATHER THAN ASSUMING: redu's extension generator ends every line with || true on purpose, so a failed package install degrades quietly instead of failing the provision. The one command that settles it is in the body of this file, and the failure is at least loud downstream: with the extension missing, migrations fail and the container never becomes healthy."
  - "⛔⛔ THE READINESS PROBE AND DJANGO READ THE DATABASE VARIABLES IN OPPOSITE ORDER, AND THAT IS WHAT WILL HANG YOUR DEPLOY. This is the highest-value line in this file. Django takes PGDATABASE before POSTGRES_DB and PGUSER before POSTGRES_USER (settings.py:136-151), so redu's injected values win there and nothing needs remapping. But the entrypoint's own wait-for-postgres takes POSTGRES_USER before PGUSER and POSTGRES_DB before PGDATABASE (docker/shared/entrypoint-common.sh:20-22), and docker/aio/env-setup.sh:19-21 always fills those in with \"adventure\" and \"database\" when they are unset. redu's managed Postgres defaults to database `app` and user `appuser`, so the probe authenticates as a user that does not exist, forever, printing 'PostgreSQL is unavailable - sleeping' once a second while Django itself would have connected fine. THE FIX IS ONE LINE PER VARIABLE: in the compose, set POSTGRES_DB to the injected PGDATABASE, POSTGRES_USER to PGUSER and POSTGRES_PASSWORD to PGPASSWORD. (The alternative is to pass db_name 'database' and db_user 'adventure' to deploy_compose so redu provisions matching names; either works, and doing NEITHER is the failure.)"
  - "POSTGRES_PASSWORD IS REQUIRED AND IT OVERWRITES PGPASSWORD. docker/aio/env-setup.sh:24-28 exits 1 with 'POSTGRES_PASSWORD is required for Standard Deployment' when it is empty, and then unconditionally sets PGPASSWORD from it. So passing only redu's injected PGPASSWORD gives you a container that refuses to start, and passing a DIFFERENT value in POSTGRES_PASSWORD silently overrides the correct one. Set POSTGRES_PASSWORD to the injected PGPASSWORD and the problem disappears in both directions."
  - "⛔ SET SECRET_KEY EXPLICITLY, OR EVERY RESTART LOGS EVERY USER OUT AND NOTHING WARNS YOU. docker/aio/env-setup.sh:30-32: if SECRET_KEY is unset the entrypoint generates a fresh random one with secrets.token_urlsafe(50) at every container start. The Standard .env.example does not even list the variable, and says everything else is 'derived automatically at startup', which is true and is exactly the trap: derived means NEW each time. Django signs sessions and password-reset tokens with it. Generate one long random value, pass it as SECRET_KEY, and pass the SAME one on every redeploy."
  - "⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: AN ADMIN IS CREATED AT DEPLOY TIME FROM ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES, AND THE SHIPPED DEFAULT IS THE WORD ADMIN AS BOTH USERNAME AND PASSWORD. docker/shared/entrypoint-common.sh:39-66 creates a Django superuser from DJANGO_ADMIN_USERNAME, DJANGO_ADMIN_PASSWORD and DJANGO_ADMIN_EMAIL when that username does not already exist, and marks its allauth email address verified so it can log in immediately. docker/aio/env-setup.sh:34-36 defaults all three, and upstream's Standard Deployment page prints the default login in plain text. This is the SAFE shape, deploy-time creation rather than a race with the first visitor, but ONLY if you actually set the values: leave them alone and you have published an instance whose administrator credential is in the documentation. GENERATE AN ALPHANUMERIC PASSWORD, at least 24 characters. Alphanumeric is not fussiness: the password is interpolated into a Python heredoc in that same shell function, so a quote or a backslash is a syntax error, not a login failure."
  - "⛔ REGISTRATION IS OPEN BY DEFAULT. settings.py:279 reads DISABLE_REGISTRATION and defaults it to false, so between the deploy going healthy and you noticing, anyone with the URL can create an account. Set DISABLE_REGISTRATION=True. users/adapters.py:22-38 is what enforces it, and it deliberately still allows signup through an invitation link, which is the right way to add the people you actually want. ⚠️ DO NOT VERIFY THIS ON THE FLAG ENDPOINT ALONE. /auth/is-registration-disabled/ returns the value of the setting (users/views.py:64), which is a check that cannot fail: it will report exactly what you configured whether or not the behaviour changed. Verify on the RENDERED /signup page instead, which swaps the form for your message, and the script in the body does that with both halves."
  - "WHAT AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST CAN REACH: the landing page, the login and signup pages, /health, the static assets and the public-user listing. AdventureLog has a real permission model behind that, and with registration closed there is no way for a stranger to obtain an account. Adventures, collections and photos are per-user and private unless their owner marks them public. Media is served through an nginx internal location (docker/shared/nginx-aio.conf), so a protected image is not fetchable by guessing its URL."
  - "SITE_URL IS THE ONLY URL VARIABLE YOU NEED, AND IT HAS TO BE THE https ONE. docker/aio/env-setup.sh:9-13 derives ORIGIN, FRONTEND_URL, PUBLIC_URL and CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS from it, so setting it correctly configures four things and setting it wrong breaks four things: CSRF rejections on login, OAuth callbacks pointing at localhost, and media URLs that do not resolve. settings.py:191-192 also switch SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE and CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE on ONLY when the value starts with https, so an http value on an https hostname ships cookies without the Secure flag. Generate the dname yourself UP FRONT, in full adventurelog-<8 lowercase alnum>.redu.cloud form, and set SITE_URL to https://<that name> with no trailing slash. A bare label gets a random suffix appended by redu and will not match."
  - "⛔ THE FIRST BOOT DOWNLOADS THE WORLD, AND IT IS WHY THE VM IS SIZED THE WAY IT IS. docker/shared/entrypoint-common.sh:69-84 runs download-countries on every start unless SKIP_WORLD_DATA=1. It fetches dr5hn's countries, states and cities dataset (version pinned at settings.py:470) from raw.githubusercontent.com, streams it through a temporary SQLite file into Postgres, and pulls one flag image per country from flagcdn.com into media storage. UPSTREAM'S OWN WORDS: 'first boot may take several minutes; ensure ~2GB RAM is available', and the script treats exit code 137 as an out-of-memory kill and stops the container. So: the VM needs outbound internet to GitHub and flagcdn on first boot, the first boot is minutes not seconds, and redu's health probe must be allowed to wait it out. If it does get OOM-killed, the two remedies are a larger flavor or SKIP_WORLD_DATA=1, the second of which costs you the world-travel feature until you run the command by hand later."
  - "PERSIST /code/media OR YOU LOSE EVERY PHOTO AND EVERY FLAG. settings.py:224 defaults MEDIA_STORAGE to local, so trip photos, avatars and the country flags downloaded on first boot all live on the app VM's filesystem, not in Postgres. Without a volume they vanish on the next redeploy while the database still lists them, and the first boot re-downloads every flag. S3 or an S3-compatible bucket is supported as an alternative (MEDIA_STORAGE=s3 plus the AWS_* variables) and is the right answer for anyone storing a lot of photos, but it is a decision to put to the user with its own cost, not a default."
  - "PORT 8015 ON THE HOST, 80 IN THE CONTAINER. The image runs its own nginx (docker/shared/nginx-aio.conf) which serves /static/, guards media through an internal location, sends /media, /admin and /accounts to Django on 8000 and everything else to the SvelteKit server on 3000. Publish host 8015 onto container 80 and pass port 8015 to deploy_compose. Do not try to expose Django or the frontend directly: neither serves the whole application on its own. nginx also carries client_max_body_size 100M, which is the real cap on a photo upload."
  - "THE HEALTH ENDPOINT IS A REAL ONE, WHICH IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE MOST ARE NOT. GET /health is answered by the frontend (frontend/src/routes/health/+server.ts) and it returns 200 with {\"ok\":true,\"backend\":\"reachable\"} ONLY after it has confirmed Django is reachable, and 503 otherwise. So it is a genuine gate for both halves of the container, and a script can assert on the body rather than on the status code alone."
  - "THE MAP NEEDS NO API KEY, AND GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY IS NOT ABOUT TILES. This is the question nobody documents for a travel app, so here is the answer. frontend/src/lib/index.ts:971-975: the DEFAULT basemap is a CARTO GL style served from basemaps.cartocdn.com, voyager in light mode and dark-matter in dark, keyless, and fetched by the VISITOR'S BROWSER rather than by your VM. The style switcher (:860-968) adds OpenStreetMap raster, OpenTopoMap, OpenFreeMap Liberty, more CARTO variants and USGS topo, all keyless too, with terrain elevation tiles from an AWS open-data bucket. ⚠️ ONE option in that list, the MapTiler 3D terrain one, carries a placeholder key whose value literally reads as an instruction to get your own: choose that basemap without supplying a real MapTiler key and you get a blank map, and it is the only way to get one here. # Self-host AdventureLog on redu

A travel journal and trip planner that is actually yours: log where you have been on a world map,
plan what is next, attach photos and notes. One container on one VM, a managed PostGIS database
beside it, and a public HTTPS URL.

## What this deploys

- **AdventureLog 0.13.0** from its official all-in-one image, pinned: the SvelteKit frontend, the
  Django backend and nginx in one container on one m1.medium VM, published on port 8015.
- **Managed Postgres with the PostGIS extension**, on its own private VM. AdventureLog cannot run
  on a plain Postgres, and redu installs the extension at provision time rather than leaving you
  to do it by hand.
- A volume on `/code/media`, which holds your photos and the country flags.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.045/hour, roughly GBP 33 a month including the database, and it fits inside the no-card
free trial.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy AdventureLog on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## Who is the administrator

**An account created at deploy time from three environment variables**, which is the safe shape:
there is no race with the first visitor to find the URL. The catch is the other half. Upstream
defaults all three to the word `admin` and prints that default login in its own installation
guide, so a deploy that leaves them alone publishes an instance whose administrator credential is
in the documentation.

So this recipe sets `DJANGO_ADMIN_USERNAME`, `DJANGO_ADMIN_PASSWORD` and
`DJANGO_ADMIN_EMAIL` to values you generate, and closes registration
(`DISABLE_REGISTRATION=True`) so nobody else can sign up afterwards. Invitation links still work,
which is how you add the people you actually want.

Generate the password **alphanumeric**. It is interpolated into a Python heredoc inside the
entrypoint, so a quote or a backslash is a syntax error rather than a login failure.

## The three that actually break it

**PostGIS.** AdventureLog's Django database engine is the PostGIS one. Point it at a plain Postgres
and migrations fail. redu can provision the extension: pass `db_extensions: ["postgis"]`.

**The database variable ordering.** Django prefers `PGUSER` and `PGDATABASE`, which is exactly
what redu injects. The container's own wait-for-postgres loop prefers `POSTGRES_USER` and
`POSTGRES_DB`, which its entrypoint fills in with defaults of its own. Leave that alone and the
container waits for a user that does not exist, forever, while Django would have connected fine.
The compose below sets both halves to the same values.

**`SECRET_KEY`.** Leave it unset and the entrypoint invents a new random one at every start. The
app comes up perfectly and logs everybody out.

## About the map

No API key is needed and none of the tiles come from your VM. The default basemap is a CARTO style
fetched by the **visitor's browser**, and the style switcher offers OpenStreetMap, OpenTopoMap,
OpenFreeMap and USGS, all keyless.

`GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY` is optional and is about **geocoding and place search**, not tiles. Without
it, searching for a place falls back to the OpenStreetMap provider, which is fine for a personal
instance.

The one way to get a blank map here is to pick the **MapTiler 3D terrain** basemap: its URL ships
with a placeholder key that literally tells you to get your own. Either supply a real MapTiler key
or use one of the other styles.

## The compose

Two files, in one directory, uploaded together.

```yaml
services:
  app:
    image: ghcr.io/seanmorley15/adventurelog:v0.13.0
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      SITE_URL: "${AL_SITE_URL}"
      SECRET_KEY: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      # Django reads PGDATABASE/PGUSER/PGPASSWORD/PGHOST/PGPORT, which redu injects, first.
      # The entrypoint's wait-for-postgres loop reads these THREE first. Same values, both halves.
      POSTGRES_DB: "${PGDATABASE}"
      POSTGRES_USER: "${PGUSER}"
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      DJANGO_ADMIN_USERNAME: "${AL_ADMIN_USER}"
      DJANGO_ADMIN_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      DJANGO_ADMIN_EMAIL: "${AL_ADMIN_EMAIL}"
      DISABLE_REGISTRATION: "True"
      DISABLE_REGISTRATION_MESSAGE: "Registration is closed on this instance."
      ENABLE_RATE_LIMITS: "True"
      DEBUG: "False"
      GUNICORN_WORKERS: "2"
    volumes:
      - adventurelog_media:/code/media/
    ports:
      - "8015:80"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "python3", "-c", "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:80/health')"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
      # Generous on purpose: the first boot imports the world dataset before anything answers.
      start_period: 600s

volumes:
  adventurelog_media:
```

And `.env` beside it, in the same uploaded directory, because `deploy_compose` only ever
APPENDS to the project's `.env` and never edits your compose:

```env
AL_SITE_URL=https://adventurelog-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
AL_SECRET_KEY=[REDACTED:value] long random value you generate, reused on every redeploy>
AL_ADMIN_USER=<not "admin">
AL_ADMIN_EMAIL=<a real address you control>
AL_ADMIN_PASSWORD=[REDACTED:value] alphanumeric characters, alphanumeric only>
```

`PGDATABASE`, `PGUSER`, `PGPASSWORD`, `PGHOST` and `PGPORT` are appended by redu when the
managed database is provisioned. You do not write them.

## Proving it from outside

Run this once the deploy reports ready. Give it the message you configured, so the check has a
positive control it cannot fake.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prove this AdventureLog is fully up and is not taking signups from strangers.
#   ./verify-adventurelog.sh adventurelog-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud "Registration is closed on this instance."
# Exit 0 = good, 1 = a real problem, 2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting).
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: verify-adventurelog.sh <host> <disabled-message>}"
MSG="${2:?pass the DISABLE_REGISTRATION_MESSAGE you configured}"
TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT
rc=0

# 1. GATE. /health is a REAL health check here: the frontend answers 200 only after it has
#    confirmed Django is reachable, and 503 otherwise. The first boot imports a world dataset,
#    so several minutes of 502 from redu's edge or 503 from the app is "wait", not "broken".
code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/health" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/health")
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /health answered HTTP $code, not 200." >&2
  [ "$code" = "502" ] && echo "  502 from the edge while the container starts. Re-run in a few minutes." >&2
  [ "$code" = "503" ] && echo "  503 means the frontend is up but Django is not yet. Still starting, or the" >&2
  [ "$code" = "503" ] && echo "  database wiring is wrong: check the container log for 'PostgreSQL is unavailable'." >&2
  exit 2
fi
if ! grep -q '"backend":"reachable"' "$TMP/health"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 200 from /health but the body does not say the backend is reachable." >&2
  head -c 200 "$TMP/health" >&2; echo >&2
  exit 2
fi
echo "OK: frontend and Django are both up."

# 2. THE ASSERTION, ON THE RENDERED PAGE RATHER THAN ON THE FLAG.
#    ⚠️ /auth/is-registration-disabled/ reports the SETTING, so it can only ever tell you what you
#    configured. The signup page swaps the form for your message, which is the behaviour itself.
code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/signup" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/signup")
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /signup answered $code, so nothing below was evaluated." >&2
  exit 2
fi
has_msg=0; has_form=0
grep -qF "$MSG" "$TMP/signup" && has_msg=1
grep -q 'password1' "$TMP/signup" && has_form=1

if [ "$has_form" = "1" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: the signup FORM is being served. Anyone with this URL can create an account." >&2
  echo "  Redeploy with DISABLE_REGISTRATION=True." >&2
  rc=1
elif [ "$has_msg" = "1" ]; then
  echo "OK: registration is closed, and the page is serving your configured message."
else
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: neither the form nor your message is in the page." >&2
  echo "  Either the page changed or you passed a different message than you deployed." >&2
  echo "  Do not leave this instance up until you have opened /signup and looked." >&2
  exit 2
fi

exit "$rc"
```

## Proving PostGIS took

redu installs the extension with every step ending in `|| true`, deliberately, so a failure
degrades quietly rather than failing the whole provision. That means the one thing worth checking
is the one thing that cannot be checked by its absence. Run this from the app VM, where the
container already has `psql` and the credentials in its environment.

```bash
# Both halves. The version string is the positive control: an empty result from a command that
# never ran looks exactly like an empty result from a database with no PostGIS.
sudo docker compose exec -T app sh -c 'psql -h "$PGHOST" -p "${PGPORT:-5432}" -U "$PGUSER" -d "$PGDATABASE" -tAc "SELECT postgis_version();"'
# Expect something like "3.5 USE_GEOS=1 USE_PROJ=1 USE_STATS=1". An error mentioning
# "function postgis_version() does not exist" means the extension is NOT installed, and the app
# will have failed at migrate rather than started.

# And the SECRET_KEY, which is the failure that leaves no trace. Print the LENGTH, not the value.
sudo docker compose exec -T app sh -c 'printf "SECRET_KEY length: %s\n" "${#SECRET_KEY}"'
# A number in the 40s means yours reached the container. Note the entrypoint GENERATES one when
# yours is missing, so a plausible length is not by itself proof: compare it across a restart, or
# simply confirm the value you set is in the project .env on the VM.
```

**GPL-3.0**, and the distinction from AGPL matters here. GPLv3 has no network clause: running a
modified AdventureLog as a service for other people does not by itself oblige you to publish your
changes. Distributing a modified build still does. Running the official image unchanged obliges you
to nothing extra.

THE FIX IS ONE LINE PER VARIABLE: in the compose, set POSTGRES_DB to the injected PGDATABASE, POSTGRES_USER to PGUSER and POSTGRES_PASSWORD to PGPASSWORD. So passing only redu's injected PGPASSWORD gives you a container that refuses to start, and passing a DIFFERENT value in POSTGRES_PASSWORD silently overrides the correct one. Set POSTGRES_PASSWORD to the injected PGPASSWORD and the problem disappears in both directions."

The Standard .env.example does not even list the variable, and says everything else is 'derived automatically at startup', which is true and is exactly the trap: derived means NEW each time. Django signs sessions and password-reset tokens with it. Generate one long random value, pass it as SECRET_KEY, and pass the SAME one on every redeploy."

# Self-host AdventureLog on redu

A travel journal and trip planner that is actually yours: log where you have been on a world map,
plan what is next, attach photos and notes. One container on one VM, a managed PostGIS database
beside it, and a public HTTPS URL.

## What this deploys

- **AdventureLog 0.13.0** from its official all-in-one image, pinned: the SvelteKit frontend, the
  Django backend and nginx in one container on one m1.medium VM, published on port 8015.
- **Managed Postgres with the PostGIS extension**, on its own private VM. AdventureLog cannot run
  on a plain Postgres, and redu installs the extension at provision time rather than leaving you
  to do it by hand.
- A volume on `/code/media`, which holds your photos and the country flags.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.045/hour, roughly GBP 33 a month including the database, and it fits inside the no-card
free trial.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy AdventureLog on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## Who is the administrator

**An account created at deploy time from three environment variables**, which is the safe shape:
there is no race with the first visitor to find the URL. The catch is the other half. Upstream
defaults all three to the word `admin` and prints that default login in its own installation
guide, so a deploy that leaves them alone publishes an instance whose administrator credential is
in the documentation.

So this recipe sets `DJANGO_ADMIN_USERNAME`, `DJANGO_ADMIN_PASSWORD` and
`DJANGO_ADMIN_EMAIL` to values you generate, and closes registration
(`DISABLE_REGISTRATION=True`) so nobody else can sign up afterwards. Invitation links still work,
which is how you add the people you actually want.

Generate the password **alphanumeric**. It is interpolated into a Python heredoc inside the
entrypoint, so a quote or a backslash is a syntax error rather than a login failure.

## The three that actually break it

**PostGIS.** AdventureLog's Django database engine is the PostGIS one. Point it at a plain Postgres
and migrations fail. redu can provision the extension: pass `db_extensions: ["postgis"]`.

**The database variable ordering.** Django prefers `PGUSER` and `PGDATABASE`, which is exactly
what redu injects. The container's own wait-for-postgres loop prefers `POSTGRES_USER` and
`POSTGRES_DB`, which its entrypoint fills in with defaults of its own. Leave that alone and the
container waits for a user that does not exist, forever, while Django would have connected fine.
The compose below sets both halves to the same values.

**`SECRET_KEY`.** Leave it unset and the entrypoint invents a new random one at every start. The
app comes up perfectly and logs everybody out.

## About the map

No API key is needed and none of the tiles come from your VM. The default basemap is a CARTO style
fetched by the **visitor's browser**, and the style switcher offers OpenStreetMap, OpenTopoMap,
OpenFreeMap and USGS, all keyless.

`GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY` is optional and is about **geocoding and place search**, not tiles. Without
it, searching for a place falls back to the OpenStreetMap provider, which is fine for a personal
instance.

The one way to get a blank map here is to pick the **MapTiler 3D terrain** basemap: its URL ships
with a placeholder key that literally tells you to get your own. Either supply a real MapTiler key
or use one of the other styles.

## The compose

Two files, in one directory, uploaded together.

```yaml
services:
  app:
    image: ghcr.io/seanmorley15/adventurelog:v0.13.0
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      SITE_URL: "${AL_SITE_URL}"
      SECRET_KEY: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      # Django reads PGDATABASE/PGUSER/PGPASSWORD/PGHOST/PGPORT, which redu injects, first.
      # The entrypoint's wait-for-postgres loop reads these THREE first. Same values, both halves.
      POSTGRES_DB: "${PGDATABASE}"
      POSTGRES_USER: "${PGUSER}"
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      DJANGO_ADMIN_USERNAME: "${AL_ADMIN_USER}"
      DJANGO_ADMIN_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      DJANGO_ADMIN_EMAIL: "${AL_ADMIN_EMAIL}"
      DISABLE_REGISTRATION: "True"
      DISABLE_REGISTRATION_MESSAGE: "Registration is closed on this instance."
      ENABLE_RATE_LIMITS: "True"
      DEBUG: "False"
      GUNICORN_WORKERS: "2"

      - adventurelog_media:/code/media/
    ports:
      - "8015:80"

And `.env` beside it, in the same uploaded directory, because `deploy_compose` only ever
APPENDS to the project's `.env` and never edits your compose:

```env
AL_SITE_URL=https://adventurelog-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
AL_SECRET_KEY=[REDACTED:value] long random value you generate, reused on every redeploy>
AL_ADMIN_USER=<not "admin">
AL_ADMIN_EMAIL=<a real address you control>
AL_ADMIN_PASSWORD=[REDACTED:value] alphanumeric characters, alphanumeric only>
```

`PGDATABASE`, `PGUSER`, `PGPASSWORD`, `PGHOST` and `PGPORT` are appended by redu when the
managed database is provisioned. You do not write them.

## Proving it from outside

Run this once the deploy reports ready. Give it the message you configured, so the check has a
positive control it cannot fake.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prove this AdventureLog is fully up and is not taking signups from strangers.
#   ./verify-adventurelog.sh adventurelog-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud "Registration is closed on this instance."
# Exit 0 = good, 1 = a real problem, 2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting).
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: verify-adventurelog.sh <host> <disabled-message>}"
MSG="${2:?pass the DISABLE_REGISTRATION_MESSAGE you configured}"
TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT
rc=0

# 1. GATE. /health is a REAL health check here: the frontend answers 200 only after it has
#    confirmed Django is reachable, and 503 otherwise. The first boot imports a world dataset,
#    so several minutes of 502 from redu's edge or 503 from the app is "wait", not "broken".
code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/health" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/health")
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /health answered HTTP $code, not 200." >&2
  [ "$code" = "502" ] && echo "  502 from the edge while the container starts. Re-run in a few minutes." >&2
  [ "$code" = "503" ] && echo "  503 means the frontend is up but Django is not yet. Still starting, or the" >&2
  [ "$code" = "503" ] && echo "  database wiring is wrong: check the container log for 'PostgreSQL is unavailable'." >&2
  exit 2
fi
if ! grep -q '"backend":"reachable"' "$TMP/health"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 200 from /health but the body does not say the backend is reachable." >&2
  head -c 200 "$TMP/health" >&2; echo >&2
  exit 2
fi
echo "OK: frontend and Django are both up."

# 2. THE ASSERTION, ON THE RENDERED PAGE RATHER THAN ON THE FLAG.
#    ⚠️ /auth/is-registration-disabled/ reports the SETTING, so it can only ever tell you what you
#    configured. The signup page swaps the form for your message, which is the behaviour itself.
code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/signup" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/signup")
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /signup answered $code, so nothing below was evaluated." >&2
  exit 2
fi
has_msg=0; has_form=0
grep -qF "$MSG" "$TMP/signup" && has_msg=1
grep -q 'password1' "$TMP/signup" && has_form=1

if [ "$has_form" = "1" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: the signup FORM is being served. Anyone with this URL can create an account." >&2
  echo "  Redeploy with DISABLE_REGISTRATION=True." >&2
  rc=1
elif [ "$has_msg" = "1" ]; then
  echo "OK: registration is closed, and the page is serving your configured message."
else
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: neither the form nor your message is in the page." >&2
  echo "  Either the page changed or you passed a different message than you deployed." >&2
  echo "  Do not leave this instance up until you have opened /signup and looked." >&2
  exit 2
fi

exit "$rc"
```

## Proving PostGIS took

redu installs the extension with every step ending in `|| true`, deliberately, so a failure
degrades quietly rather than failing the whole provision. That means the one thing worth checking
is the one thing that cannot be checked by its absence. Run this from the app VM, where the
container already has `psql` and the credentials in its environment.

```bash
# Both halves. The version string is the positive control: an empty result from a command that
# never ran looks exactly like an empty result from a database with no PostGIS.
sudo docker compose exec -T app sh -c 'psql -h "$PGHOST" -p "${PGPORT:-5432}" -U "$PGUSER" -d "$PGDATABASE" -tAc "SELECT postgis_version();"'
# Expect something like "3.5 USE_GEOS=1 USE_PROJ=1 USE_STATS=1". An error mentioning
# "function postgis_version() does not exist" means the extension is NOT installed, and the app
# will have failed at migrate rather than started.

# And the SECRET_KEY, which is the failure that leaves no trace. Print the LENGTH, not the value.
sudo docker compose exec -T app sh -c 'printf "SECRET_KEY length: %s\n" "${#SECRET_KEY}"'
# A number in the 40s means yours reached the container. Note the entrypoint GENERATES one when
# yours is missing, so a plausible length is not by itself proof: compare it across a restart, or
# simply confirm the value you set is in the project .env on the VM.
```

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prove this AdventureLog is fully up and is not taking signups from strangers.
#   ./verify-adventurelog.sh adventurelog-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud "Registration is closed on this instance."
# Exit 0 = good, 1 = a real problem, 2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting).
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: verify-adventurelog.sh <host> <disabled-message>}"
MSG="${2:?pass the DISABLE_REGISTRATION_MESSAGE you configured}"
TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT
rc=0

# 1. GATE. /health is a REAL health check here: the frontend answers 200 only after it has
#    confirmed Django is reachable, and 503 otherwise. The first boot imports a world dataset,
#    so several minutes of 502 from redu's edge or 503 from the app is "wait", not "broken".
code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/health" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/health")
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /health answered HTTP $code, not 200." >&2
  [ "$code" = "502" ] && echo "  502 from the edge while the container starts. Re-run in a few minutes." >&2
  [ "$code" = "503" ] && echo "  503 means the frontend is up but Django is not yet. Still starting, or the" >&2
  [ "$code" = "503" ] && echo "  database wiring is wrong: check the container log for 'PostgreSQL is unavailable'." >&2
  exit 2
fi
if ! grep -q '"backend":"reachable"' "$TMP/health"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 200 from /health but the body does not say the backend is reachable." >&2
  head -c 200 "$TMP/health" >&2; echo >&2
  exit 2
fi
echo "OK: frontend and Django are both up."

# 2. THE ASSERTION, ON THE RENDERED PAGE RATHER THAN ON THE FLAG.
